title: Progression in Running Intensity or Running Volume and the Development of Specific Injuries in Recreational Runners: Run Clever, a Randomized Trial Using Competing Risks
authors: Ramskov D, Rasmussen S, Sørensen H, Parner ET, Lind M, Nielsen R
journal: Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy
population: Healthy recreational runners (not specifically novices), 24-week follow-up: 8-week preconditioning then 16 weeks of an intensity-progression (S-I) or volume-progression (S-V) schedule
findings: Of 447 runners, 80 sustained an injury (S-I n=36, S-V n=44).
The S-I group progressed high-intensity running (88% VO2max or greater) each week; the S-V group progressed total weekly running volume.
Risk differences for hypothesised intensity-related injuries in the S-I group were -0.8% (-5.0, 3.4) at 2 weeks and -5.1% (-16.5, 6.3) at 16 weeks; all reported confidence intervals included zero.
The authors concluded there was no difference in risk of hypothesised intensity- and volume-specific injuries between the two schedules.
limitations: Likely underpowered for 16-week differences (wide CIs); recreational rather than novice runners; both arms had an 8-week preconditioning phase, so the benefit of preconditioning itself was not tested. Specific injuries were hypothesised from clinical assumptions.
implications: No evidence supports separate injury-risk rules for intensity vs volume progression or modelling Achilles/plantar injuries as intensity-specific.

Progressing either high-intensity running or weekly volume (one at a time) is acceptable in a 16-week block. An 8-week low-intensity preconditioning phase was the trial's design, not a tested benefit, so treat it as a conservative option for new runners.
